title: When every cache misses at once
teaches: Thundering herds and stale sets, leases, invalidation from the database's log, and caches across regions

parts.title: Two and a half hours in September

blocks.text: On Thursday 23 September 2010 Facebook went down for about two and a half hours, its worst outage in four years. That evening Robert Johnson, who ran its software engineering, posted an account of what had happened, and it is short enough to retell in full.[^johnson]

Facebook kept some configuration values in its [[memcache|cache]] servers, copied from a cluster of databases. An automated system watched those cached values, and when a web server found one that looked invalid, it fixed it: it queried the database for the persistent copy and wrote that back into the cache. That day an engineer changed the persistent copy of one value, and the new value was one the checker took to be invalid. So every web server that read it saw an invalid value and set out to fix it, and every fix was a query to the same database cluster. Hundreds of thousands of queries a second arrived at a cluster built for far fewer.

The cluster slowed, then began returning errors. The fixing code read an error from the database as one more invalid value, so it deleted the cached key and tried again. Now the deletes guaranteed misses, the misses produced queries, and the queries produced errors. Reverting the bad value did not stop it, because the loop no longer needed the bad value to keep going. In the end the engineers had to stop all traffic to that database cluster, which meant turning the site off, and bring it back slowly.

Throughout, look for a [[feedback loop|busy]]: a response to trouble that makes more of the same trouble. A cache is especially prone to one, because it sits in front of something slower and more fragile than itself, and the moment it fails to answer, the work it was absorbing goes straight to the thing behind it. This lesson is about the cache's own misses: the hot key that expires, the value that goes stale behind everyone's back, and the delete that never arrives.

Take one **hot key**, a key that is read far more than the rest: a celebrity's profile, a front-page story, a configuration value every page needs. Say 1,000 web servers read it 20,000 times a second between them. It is held in memcache in front of a database, used cache-aside as lesson 5 described: read the cache; on a miss, query the database and set the result in the cache.

First the numbers. While the key is in the cache, the database never hears about it. When it expires or is deleted, the next reader misses and sends a query. If that query takes 50 ms, the key stays missing for those 50 ms, and in that time 20,000 × 0.05 = 1,000 more readers miss and each sends the same query. That burst of identical misses is a **thundering herd**. A thousand copies of one query is wasteful, and if the database stayed as fast under the herd as it was before it, the waste would end after 50 ms.

It does not stay as fast. Lesson 2 showed that waiting time grows without bound as a server nears full load. Suppose the database can run 100 queries at full speed at once, about 2,000 of these queries a second. Given more than 100, it shares its time evenly among them, so with 1,000 in flight each runs at a tenth of its speed: a model called **processor sharing**.[^ps] The herd asks for 20,000 a second. The first query, the one whose answer would end the herd, now shares the database with hundreds and then thousands of copies of itself, and each slows as more arrive. Slower answers mean a longer miss, and a longer miss means more copies. Make a guess before you run it.

blocks.caption: A hot key expires. The database model shares its time among the queries it holds, so a big herd slows the query that would end it. Illustrative numbers.
blocks.task: Guess, then turn leases on and play the two seconds through

blocks.text: At 2,000 reads a second the herd is 100 queries and the key is back in 50 ms. At 4,000 it is about 270 queries and 70 ms. At 10,000 it is several thousand queries and over half a second. At 20,000 the first query takes about 40 seconds to finish, and in that time the herd grows to hundreds of thousands. The change from harmless to collapse comes over a factor of ten in traffic, and the threshold is where the herd's queries pass what the database can serve.

Two designs make this worse, and both are common. The first gives hot keys a short **time to live** (TTL), so they expire every few seconds to stay fresh; each expiry is a fresh herd. The second retries on error, the loop that turned Facebook off in 2010: once the database begins to fail, every retry adds a query to a server that is failing because it has too many.

In April 2013, at the NSDI conference in Lombard, Illinois, Rajesh Nishtala and his colleagues described how Facebook had built memcache into a system serving billions of requests a second over trillions of cached items: "Scaling Memcache at Facebook". One of the first problems they took on was the herd, and the tool they used was a **lease**.

In GFS, the master handed a chunk's primary a lease (lesson 7), and lesson 11's leader held one: a right, granted for a limited time, that lets one party act and makes everyone else hold back. Facebook's lease is the same idea at the size of one key. When a client misses, memcache gives it a [[lease token|clock]], a 64-bit number bound to that key. The token is the right to fill the key: a client that sets the key must present it.

The herd stops because memcache hands out a token for a given key at most once every 10 seconds. The first client to miss gets one and goes to the database. Every other client that misses in the next 10 seconds gets no token, only a note to wait a short while and read the cache again. The holder usually sets the value within a few milliseconds, so the waiters' second read is a hit. A herd of thousands becomes one query and a few thousand cheap cache reads. If the holder dies or never sets the value, the waiters go on missing until the 10 seconds are up, when the next miss gets a fresh token: a few seconds of waiting on one key is the price of never having a herd. In the figure, turning leases on keeps the database at one query however fast the key is read. The paper reports that leases cut the peak rate of database queries for a hot key from about 17,000 a second to 1,300.[^peak]

For data where a slightly old answer is fine, memcache offers a shortcut. When a key is deleted, its old value is kept briefly in a side list, and a waiting client can take that value, marked as stale, instead of waiting at all. This is a trade made for each kind of data: a feed can show a value a second old, a privacy setting should not.

There are other ways to break up a herd, and they work at different places. A single web server can make sure it has only one query in flight per key, and make its other threads wait for that answer, which is called **request coalescing**; it shrinks a herd of 1,000 to one query per web server, still 1,000 queries if all 1,000 web servers miss together. A cache can also refresh a hot key a little before it expires, chosen at random for each reader, so the refresh is done by one early reader instead of all late ones.[^early] The lease works across every client, because the cache itself decides who fills the key.

Lesson 5 explained why a writer deletes the cached key instead of setting the new value: two writers setting values can arrive at the cache in the opposite order from the database, and the cache keeps the older one. Deleting avoids that, and a delete can be repeated safely, since deleting a deleted key changes nothing. There remains one race, between a reader and a writer, that deleting does not prevent. The paper calls it a **stale set**: a client puts a value in the cache that is no longer the latest.

In the figure, reader A misses on a key and is given lease token 7, then reads the old value, v1, from the database and stalls. Writer B then commits the new value, v2, to the database and deletes the key from the cache. Finally A wakes and tries to set v1.

blocks.caption: The stale set, step by step: a slow reader fills the cache after a writer has deleted it.
blocks.task: Play it with leases off, then with leases on

blocks.text: The stale value is the worst kind, because nothing will correct it. The delete has already happened, so the cache holds v1 until the key is written again or expires, and for a value that rarely changes that may be days. Leases fix it at no extra cost. The delete that B sends voids any token memcache has handed out for that key, so when A arrives with token 7, memcache knows that the value A carries may predate a write, and refuses it. The next reader misses, gets a new token, and reads v2.

A lease does not make the cache always right. Between B's write to the database and B's delete, readers still get v1 from the cache, for a few milliseconds. What the lease guarantees is that every stale value is short-lived: once the delete arrives, no older value can be put back.

So far the web server that wrote to the database also deleted the key. That works until it doesn't. A web server can crash after its commit and before its delete, and then the old value stays cached with nothing to remove it. And Facebook ran several **front-end clusters** in each region, each with its own memcache servers holding copies of the same keys; a write must delete the key in every one of them, and a web server does not know which hold it.

Facebook's answer was to take deletes from the one place that knows about every committed write: the database's [[commit log|write]]. Lesson 4 met this log as the stream replicas apply. A MySQL server records each committed change, in commit order, in its binary log. A web server that ran a write worked out which cached keys it made stale and embedded their names in the SQL statement, so they were recorded in the log with the change. A daemon called **mcsqueal**, running beside each database, read the commit log, pulled out those keys, batched them, and sent the deletes to every memcache cluster in the region through a set of routers.

This changes the guarantee. A delete taken from the log is sent only for a write that committed, and it is sent even if the web server that made the write has crashed, because the log outlives the server. A delete can still be late, but it will not be lost: if the daemon crashes it starts again from its place in the log. And since a delete voids any lease token on the key, a slow reader in some cluster cannot put an older value back after it: the stale-set rule again. The cost is a little delay, the time to read the log and send the batch. Batching also saved the network: deletes for many keys went out in one packet, to one router per cluster, where sending them one by one from each web server would have meant millions of small packets. The principle reaches well past caches: any copy of data (a cache, a search index, a replica) is kept right most simply by following the source's own record of changes, and lesson 16 builds a whole system on that idea.

The paper has one more answer to a cache's misses, for the case where a memcache server dies. Lesson 5's consistent hashing would hand the dead server's keys to its neighbours on the ring, and with them its hot keys, which can overload a neighbour and then the next one along. Facebook instead kept a small spare pool of memcache servers, about 1% of a cluster, called the **gutter**. A client that gets no answer from a server retries at the gutter, and on a miss there fills the gutter from the database. The dead server's keys miss once each into the gutter and are then served from it, instead of falling on the database for as long as the server is down. Gutter entries expire within seconds, which stands in for invalidation, since deletes are not sent to the gutter.[^udp]

Facebook served users from datacentres in several **regions**, far apart. One region was the primary: it held the master databases, which took every write. The others held read-only replicas of those databases, kept up to date by replication, and their web servers read from their own replicas and caches. Lesson 4's replication lag returns here at the scale of an ocean: a change committed in the US can take a second or more to reach a replica in Europe.

Combine lag with a cache, and a user can undo their own change. The figure has the two fixes described below as switches, "Deletes from the commit log" and "Remote marker". Play it with both off first.

blocks.caption: A user in a replica region saves a change and reads it back. Times are illustrative; real replication lag across an ocean is often a second or more.
blocks.task: Turn on both fixes and play it to the end

blocks.text: Two things go wrong, one after the other. First, the user's own read misses the cache and reads the local replica, which has not yet applied the write, so they see their change undone. Second, that read puts the old value back in the cache, where everyone keeps reading it after the replica has caught up. Taking deletes from the commit log fixes the second: the European replica's own daemon sends the delete after the replica has applied the write, so no copy older than the replica's data can outlive it. It does nothing for the user's first read, which happens before the replica has caught up.

For that, Facebook used a **remote marker**. Before the write, the web server sets a marker key for k in its region's cache, and the marker is removed when the replicated write arrives. A reader that misses on k and finds the marker reads from the primary region instead of the local replica. That read is slower, a round trip across the ocean of perhaps 100 ms, but it happens only for keys written in the last moment, and it gives the person who made the change their own change back. Lesson 4 called this property reading your own writes; lesson 13 placed it among the consistency models. Facebook chose it for writers and left everyone else with eventual consistency, a trade made openly: the paper says it accepts stale reads for most data in return for serving from local replicas.

Memcache in front of MySQL was not the end of the story. In 2013 Facebook also described TAO, a cache built for its social graph of objects and the links between them, which reads through to the database itself and applies a client's writes to its own cached copy, so most of the races in this lesson cannot start.[^tao]

blocks.caption: Six questions on herds, leases and invalidation
blocks.task: Choose the best answer to each

items.ask: A key is read 20,000 times a second. Its refill query takes 50 ms on an idle database, which can serve about 2,000 such queries a second. Why can its expiry keep it missing for many seconds?
choices: Every miss queries the database, and the copies slow the one query whose answer would refill the key
Memcache refuses to store a key while other clients are still reading it, so the refill waits for a quiet moment
The cache evicts the key again as soon as it is set, because thousands of clients are asking for it at once
items.why: In 50 ms a thousand readers miss, ten times what the database can serve, and the database shares its time among them. The refill query slows, the miss lasts longer, and more readers pile in: a feedback loop.

items.ask: How do memcache leases stop a thundering herd on a hot key?
choices: They give every client that misses a token, and the database answers token holders in the order they arrived
They hand out a token for a key at most once every 10 seconds, and clients without one wait and read the cache again
They make the cache keep a hot key for ever, so that it never expires and never needs to be refilled
items.why: Only the token holder queries the database. The rest are told to wait a few milliseconds, by which time the holder has usually set the value, so their second read is a hit.

items.ask: Reader A misses, reads v1 from the database, and stalls. Writer B commits v2 and deletes the key. A then sets v1. With leases, what happens?
choices: Memcache keeps v1, since A was the first to miss and so holds the oldest and strongest claim to the key
Memcache stores v1 but marks it stale, and the next reader replaces it with v2 straight away
Memcache refuses A's set, because B's delete voided the lease token that A was given on its miss
items.why: A delete voids outstanding leases on that key. A's value may predate the write, so it is refused, and the next reader gets a fresh token and reads v2.

items.ask: Why did Facebook send cache invalidations from a daemon reading the database's commit log rather than from the web servers that made the writes?
choices: The log lists every committed write and outlives a crashed web server, so no delete is lost, and the deletes can be batched
Reading the log is faster than sending a delete from the web server, so stale values are removed sooner than before
Web servers sent deletes over UDP, which loses packets, while the daemon's deletes go over TCP and so always arrive
items.why: A web server can crash between its commit and its delete, and does not know every cluster that holds the key. The log has every committed write, in order, and is read again from its last place after a crash. Deletes from it arrive a little later, not sooner.

items.ask: What problem does a small gutter pool of spare memcache servers solve?
choices: It holds the cache's least-used keys so that the main servers have more memory free for the hot ones
It takes the load of a failed memcache server, so its keys neither hit the database nor overload a neighbour
It stores the recently deleted values that leases hand to waiting clients as stale but acceptable answers
items.why: Rehashing a dead server's keys onto its neighbours can push hot keys onto a server that then fails too. The gutter, about 1% of the servers, absorbs them, with short expiry standing in for invalidation.

items.ask: In a region that reads from a lagging replica, a user saves a change and reloads the page straight away. Which design shows them their change?
choices: Deleting the key from the local cache as soon as the write commits in the primary region
Taking deletes from the local replica's commit log, so the cache is cleared once the replica has the write
A remote marker set before the write, so a miss on that key reads from the primary region until the replica catches up
items.why: The first two clear the cache, but the user's miss still reads the local replica, which has not applied the write. The marker sends just that reader, for just that key, to the primary.

items.ask: On 23 September 2010 reverting the bad configuration value did not end Facebook's outage. Why not?
choices: The bad value had already been copied to every replica, and replication could not be stopped while the site was running
Clients treated database errors as invalid values and deleted the key, so the overload kept producing more queries
The engineers could not find which value was bad until the site was turned off and the logs could be read
items.why: The loop had become self-sustaining: overload caused errors, errors caused deletes, deletes caused misses, misses caused queries. Only stopping the traffic broke it.

summary: **A miss on a hot key is a herd.** Every reader that misses in the time a refill takes sends its own query, so a 50 ms refill of a key read 20,000 times a second sends a thousand.
**A herd can feed itself.** When the copies outnumber what the database can serve, they slow the very query that would end the herd, and the miss stretches from milliseconds to seconds.
**Look for feedback loops.** Facebook's 2010 outage was a fix that queried the database on every error, and errors came from those queries; only turning traffic off broke it.
**A lease gives one client the right to refill a key.** Memcache hands out a token per key at most every 10 seconds; the rest wait a moment and read the cache again.
**The same lease stops stale sets.** A delete voids outstanding tokens, so a slow reader cannot put back a value that a writer has replaced.
**Invalidate from the commit log.** A daemon reading the database's log sends a delete for every committed write, even if the writer crashed, and batches them.
**A gutter pool catches a dead cache server's keys.** About 1% spare servers keep its load off the database and off its neighbours.
**Lag and caches together can undo a user's change.** A remote marker sends the writer's own reads to the primary region until the replica catches up.

johnson.title: The post
johnson.text: Johnson's post, "More Details on Today's Outage", opens by saying the site had been down or unreachable for many people for about 2.5 hours and ends with an apology. It is one of the earliest public accounts of a feedback loop taking down a large site, and it is short: about a page.

ps.title: The database in the figure
ps.text: Processor sharing is a simplification. Real databases also queue at connection limits, time queries out and run out of memory, which tends to make collapse sharper. The numbers show the shape of the threshold, not Facebook's.

peak.title: Seventeen thousand to thirteen hundred
peak.text: The paper gives this as a measured peak for keys that see heavy reads and writes. The figure's one-query answer is the ideal; in practice tokens expire, holders fail, and different keys refill at once.

early.title: Refreshing early at random
early.text: In 2015 Andrea Vattani, Flavio Chierichetti and Keegan Lowenstein showed how to choose when to refresh: each reader recomputes early with a probability that rises sharply near expiry and grows with how long the recomputation takes. Most reads never recompute, and usually exactly one reader refreshes just before the key would have expired.

udp.title: Gets over UDP
udp.text: Facebook's web servers sent memcache reads over UDP, with no connection to set up, and treated a lost packet as a miss. Sets and deletes went over TCP through mcrouter, a proxy that also sends a write to every cluster that needs it.

tao.title: TAO
tao.text: TAO, described by Nathan Bronson and colleagues at USENIX ATC in June 2013, stores objects (people, posts, places) and associations (likes, friendships) and is tuned for the queries a social graph needs, such as the newest 50 comments on a post. Its caches are arranged in tiers with a leader cache per shard that talks to the database.
